title: Why Paying One Dollar Beat Paying Twenty?
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — Festinger & Carlsmith (1959): Turning Wooden Pegs for $1 vs $20 — Why Getting Paid LESS Changed People's Minds!, grounded in Leon Festinger, James M. Carlsmith (1959) (The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that every classical behaviorist from Thorndike to Skinner predicted an ironclad law: BIGGER REWARD = BIGGER ATTITUDE CHANGE — pay someone $20 (~$215 in today's purchasing power!) to praise a boring chore and they should love it way more than someone paid a measly $1.

Follow-up physiological and behavioral evidence demonstrates: In 1959 at Stanford (Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology), Leon Festinger and student J. Merrill Carlsmith put 71 undergraduates through ONE FULL HOUR of deliberately soul-crushing boredom: 30 minutes lifting 12 spools onto and off a tray with one hand, followed by 30 minutes turning 48 square wooden pegs a quarter-turn clockwise over and over while an experimenter clicked a stopwatch.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Leon Festinger, James M. Carlsmith (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0041593
- Joel Cooper, Russell H. Fazio (1984). A New Look at Dissonance Theory. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0065-2601(08)60121-5
- Daryl J. Bem (1967). Self-perception: An alternative interpretation of cognitive dissonance phenomena. Psychological Review. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0024835

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
